challenges.name: ttl-swr-evidence
challenges.title: TTL & stale-while-revalidate: read the headers and the log
challenges.description: Two statements on the leaderboard cache: what a CDN does with a stale response inside its stale-while-revalidate window, and what a stale-while-revalidate patch without single flight does to the database.

questions.question:
Response of GET https://app.codedev.test/api/leaderboard, stored by the CDN at 10:00:00:
cache-control: public, max-age=0, s-maxage=60, stale-while-revalidate=300

The origin is healthy and the CDN supports stale-while-revalidate. A learner requests the same URL at 10:03:00.

Statement: "The CDN answers at once with the stored response, now 180 seconds old, and fetches a fresh copy from the origin in the background."
questions.explanation: True. For a shared cache the freshness lifetime is s-maxage=60, so at 180 seconds the response is stale, but it is still inside the stale-while-revalidate window (60 + 300 = 360 seconds). Inside that window the cache may answer with the stale response immediately and revalidate it in the background; the next request after the refresh gets the new copy. At 10:06:00 or later the response would be beyond the window and the request would wait for the origin. max-age=0 only concerns the browser. The misconception is that a response past its max-age always means waiting for the origin; that is the plain-TTL cliff the extension exists to avoid.

questions.question:
lib/cache.ts (second patch):
if (entry && age >= maxAge && age < maxAge + staleWhileRevalidate) {
  refresh(key);          // starts db.weeklyLeaderboard() in the background
  return entry.value;
}

Server log at the 09:00 peak:
09:01:00.004  cache STALE leaderboard:weekly age=60.00s -> background refresh started
09:01:00.051  cache STALE leaderboard:weekly age=60.05s -> background refresh started
...
09:01:01.962  cache STALE leaderboard:weekly age=61.96s -> background refresh started   (40 in total)

Statement: "Because all 40 requests were answered at once with the stale value, the database received a single leaderboard query at 09:01."
questions.explanation: False. Answering at once is about latency; the log shows the load: each of the 40 stale requests started its own background refresh, because the code never checks whether a refresh for the key is already running. The database still runs 40 copies of the 2-second query, just without anyone waiting for them. The fix is single flight: remember the running fetch per key, let stale requests skip starting another, and let waiting requests join it. The misconception is that stale-while-revalidate by itself protects the origin; it removes waiting, not load.

challenges.name: ttl-stale-while-revalidate
challenges.title: TTL and stale-while-revalidate
challenges.description:
The CodeDev weekly leaderboard query takes about 2 seconds. With a plain 60-second TTL, the first request after each expiry waits for it, and at the 09:00 peak forty requests arrive in that window and start forty identical queries. Write SwrCache, a cache with maxAge and staleWhileRevalidate on a fake clock (seconds), that serves stale values while it revalidates, starts at most one fetch per key, and keeps serving the stale value when a revalidation fails.

new SwrCache(maxAge, staleWhileRevalidate, clock, origin): throw Error("invalid cache config") if either number is negative or not finite. get(key) returns a Promise<Served> with { status, value, error, fetchesStarted }. The age of a stored value is clock.now() minus the time its fetch completed. (1) age < maxAge: HIT, the stored value, no fetch. (2) maxAge <= age < maxAge + staleWhileRevalidate: STALE, the stored value at once, and start a background revalidation unless a fetch for this key is already running (fetchesStarted 1 if this request started it, else 0). (3) No stored value, or age >= maxAge + staleWhileRevalidate: MISS, wait for a fetch: join the fetch already running for the key (fetchesStarted 0), or start one (1). There is never more than one fetch per key at a time.

A successful fetch stores its value, dated at its completion time, and every MISS waiting on it gets that value. A failed fetch stores nothing and keeps the old value (stale-if-error until the stale window ends): later STALE requests keep getting the old value and the next one starts a new revalidation. A MISS waiting on a failed fetch gets { status: "MISS", value: null, error: <the error message> }. A failed background revalidation must not reject anything that nobody awaits. Keys are independent.

The runner: the n-th fetch of a key gets the n-th scripted answer of that key ({ value, takes } or { error, takes }) takes seconds after it starts; fetches that complete at time t are processed before requests that arrive at time t. Input: { "maxAge": s, "staleWhileRevalidate": s, "origin": { "<key>": [answers] }, "requests": [{ "at": s, "key": "<key>" }, ...] }. Output, per request: t=<at> <key>: <status> "<value>" or error "<message>", fetches=<n> answered t=<time>; then the number of fetches per key, or "error: <message>" if the constructor throws.
hints: A request can find a key in four situations: nothing stored, fresh, stale, expired; and independently, a fetch for that key may already be running. Which of these combinations start a new fetch, and which ones must wait for one?

Look at what you need to remember per key besides the value: the time its fetch completed (not started), and the promise of the fetch that is running right now, if any. Remove that promise when the fetch settles, on success and on failure, and decide what happens to the stored value in each case.

A similar timeline with maxAge 10 and a stale window of 20, where a fetch takes 3 s: t=0 MISS starts a fetch and is answered at t=3; t=12 is a HIT (age 9); t=14 is STALE and starts a refresh that completes at t=17; t=15 is STALE with no new fetch; t=18 is a HIT on the new value (age 1). Had the refresh failed at t=17, t=18 would still be STALE on the old value and would start the next refresh.
